title: EU AI Act Article 49 — Post-Market Monitoring Plan Requirements for High-Risk AI
context: 2026-08-29 engine cycle — answer-first seed page for the Council of AI compliance knowledge base; Article 49 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI system and the risks
body: EU AI Act Article 49 mandates that providers of high-risk AI systems establish, implement, document, and maintain a post-market monitoring (PMM) system. This is not a one-time certification checkbox — it is a living obligation that runs for the lifetime of the system in the Union market. The PMM system must actively and systematically collect, document, and analyse relevant data provided by users or gathered through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime, and must allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of the AI system with the AI Act. Three core requirements structure the obligation. (1) The PMM plan must be proportionate to the nature of the AI technology and the risks — a general-purpose medical diagnostic AI and a narrow industrial quality-control classifier will have materially different PMM scopes, frequencies, and data sources. (2) The plan must specify how post-market data flows back to the risk management system under Article 9 — findings from the field must update the risk register, not sit in a separate silo. (3) Serious incidents and malfunctioning must trigger the Article 62 reporting obligation, meaning the PMM system is the primary sensor network that feeds the incident reporting pipeline. The practical challenge for providers is the data gap: post-market monitoring requires real-world performance telemetry, but high-risk AI systems often operate in environments the provider does not directly control — a hospital, a factory floor, a court registry. The Council of AI posture addresses this through monitored containment: every inference, output, and boundary crossing is time-stamped, logged, and attributed, so the PMM system is not guessing from user complaints but reading from a signed, verifiable telemetry stream. A verified measurement credential wraps each measurement event, giving an auditor a checkable chain from the PMM plan to the actual field data. For providers building their Article 49 compliance package, the honest answer is: you cannot claim to monitor what you cannot measure. The verified measurement credential closes that gap — it proves that a measurement was taken at a specific moment, by a specific operator, and was not altered afterward. That is the difference between a PMM plan that passes a desk audit and one that survives a field inspection.
